sections.title: Policy and access to the centre
sections.text:
Utrecht is steadily taking cars out of its centre and charging more for the street space that is left. The city's street rates in 2026 are €8.01 an hour in zone A1 (the centre), €6.94 in A2 and €5.34 in zones B and C, above its garage rates, which are €2.85 an hour at De Grifthoek and €4.68 at Kruisstraat [22]. On 25 April 2024 a majority of the council voted to introduce paid parking throughout the city over about twelve years, roughly 10,000 addresses a year [12]. The municipality proposed in September 2025 to postpone the second block of that roll-out by six months, to 1 November 2026 [17]. Resident permit prices have been raised repeatedly. In 2020 the city proposed raising the A1 permit to €36.84 a month from April 2021 [4], after announcing in 2018 rises of 10% in tariffs, 20% in resident permits and 15% in business permits [0].

The city also removes spaces. It has said it aims to remove 750 to 1,500 spaces a year (0.5 to 1% of the total) and create parking hubs at the city edge [6]. Its 'binnenstad autoluw' page lists spaces removed in 2021 to 2025 (14, 13, 16, 50 and 103), with about 50 more planned for 2026 [23]. In late 2025 it removed 53 spaces on the Oudegracht and in Twijnstraat [18] and 35 at Janskerkhof [20]. For new buildings, the 2021 parking norms, in force until April 2025, allowed no on-site parking in the city centre [7]. Catharijnesingel was closed to through traffic by cars and motorcycles between Stationsstraat and Spoorstraat from 21 September 2026, with a warning period until 1 January 2027, after which fines apply. The Hoog Catharijne garages stay reachable by a north and a south route [27].

sections.title: Parking developments
sections.text:
The city is shifting visitors to the edge. From 1 September 2020 its P+R garages charged €2 a day for users who continue by public transport and €6 for parking only [3]. A council letter in November 2024 said more than three quarters of parkers in the municipal P+Rs are day visitors who do not continue by public transport. It also set 2025 tariffs, with municipal garage and P+R products up 4.5% and Westraven moved to an hourly rate of €2.94 [14][15]. For 2026 tariffs rose another 2.2%, and the Papendorp and Science Park day cards were replaced by hourly rates [19]. The university raised its Science Park P+R day rate from €7.50 to €15 from January 2026 [21]. The city says it keeps garage tariffs below street tariffs and edge-of-city parking cheaper than the centre [19]. The dynamic parking guidance system was due for replacement in 2025 [15].

New housing is built with few cars. The Merwede district, started in March 2025, has 6,000 homes and two garages at the district edge for about a third of residents' cars, at about €200 per space a month [16]. Klépierre, which owns Hoog Catharijne, is obliged to provide 3,000 bicycle spaces and 1,300 more if offices are sold, all by 1 January 2027 [8]. We found no sourced figures on a shift from the centre to shopping centres.

sections.title: Operators, positioning and utilisation
sections.text:
Utrecht's garages are run by the city, Q-Park and Interparking. Our price list covers 41 garages. The municipality runs 7 of them (2,687 spaces), Q-Park 4 (1,751), and the rest are listed through ParkBee with no capacity. Interparking runs Hoog Catharijne's P5 with 1,174 spaces, at €2.00 for the first 20 minutes then €1.00 per 10 minutes and €45 for 24 hours [24]. Klépierre lists 3,500 parking places at Hoog Catharijne [25]. Prices fall steeply with distance from the Domplein: the two garages within 500 m have a median of €7.12 an hour, against €4.68 up to 1 km, €3.58 up to 2 km and €3.60 beyond.

Our measured set is six garages with 2,769 spaces. They averaged 32% on weekdays and 35% at weekends from August to early October 2026, so these garages are busier at weekends. The fullest is the municipal De Grifthoek (73% on weekdays, 71% at weekends), at a rate of €2.85 an hour [22], far above the others: Kruisstraat 36%, Radboud 32%, Stationsstraat 30%, Vredenburg 25% and Hoog Catharijne P2 14%. The data cover the summer holidays and the university break, so term-time figures may differ, and we have no multi-year history for Utrecht.
